newsitem.title: UK: Investors queue up to buy at UK gilt auction.
newsitem.headline: Investors queue up to buy at UK gilt auction.

text.p: A surge of demand at an auction of 10-year government bonds or gilts suggests British official debt could be coming back into favour, analysts said on Wednesday.
The vast majority of bids, 93 percent, were allotted at the lowest accepted price, suggesting the Bank of England had little problem shifting the supply.
Bids for the 2.5 billion stg of 7.5 percent gilts due 2006 exceeded 6.7 billion stg, giving cover of 2.69 times.
"The cover is broadly in line with the last auction of this stock and there is nice close bunching of the bids," said Stephen Lewis, director of research at London Bond Broking.
Analysts said 10-year gilts were often a favourite for investors but said the result was encouraging nonetheless.

"The 10-year sector attracts overseas investors, it's just long enough for pension and insurance funds and banks are happy to extend out that far (down the curve)," said Adam Chester, bond strategist at Yamaichi International.
Hopes that a solid recovery in British economic growth will eat into the public sector borrowing requirement and ease funding pressures provided a favourable backdrop, he added.

Steve Scott, gilts analyst at Kleinwort Benson, said auctions have been well received over the past six months. Gone were the days of last year when one gilt auction failed to attract sufficient cover for the first time in living memory.
"People have gained confidence in the auction system over the last six months," he said on Reuters Financial Television.
The Bank itself has helped build that confidence by announcing in advance roughly at what maturities it will issue gilts each quarter.
"The changes the Bank put through have helped," Chester said. "The market knows pretty much what's coming and can create a short base ahead of the event."

Scott said the latest gilt sale left the Bank of England well placed in relation to its supply schedule for the current financial year. "According to the Bank's figures, they've funded about 45 percent of the requirement for this financial year. They are pretty much on target."

Lewis said the recent move back up in gilt yields left them at attractive levels, adding that last week's round of European interest rate cuts, led by a 30 basis point slice off the German repo rate, had not yet been matched in Britain.

"At these levels, international confidence probably will return," Lewis said on Reuters Financial Television. "The UK is the one market where we could possibly see some good news on interest rates soon."
Lewis said the odds favoured a rate cut after the September 4 monetary meeting between Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke and Bank of England Governor Eddie George.

"If Mr Clarke fails to deliver a cut in the next month or so, he may not get another chance to do so," he said, noting the likelihood that British economic growth will accelerate and U.S. rates head higher in the not too distant future.

Traders also saw some upside for gilts, noting the gilt/Bund spread, which edged as high as 169 basis points (1.60 percent point) early on Wednesday, was now near the top of its range of the last month and more, of 160 to 170 basis points. The bund/gilt spread shows how much much more or less yield different instruments have to offer the investor. Bund --
